summary: A 1975 note discussing how the FTP CWD command should work for login access to directories that only hold files. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 697 discusses how FTP could let a user access a TENEX files-only directory with owner rights. It proposes changing FTP login rules or adding an optional password to CWD.

questions: what does cwd do in ftp
subtitle: Two proposed ways to give FTP users access to TENEX files-only directories.

tldr.problem: TENEX's FTP server does not allow an FTP login to a files-only directory, and CWD alone does not give a user owner access to that directory.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes either removing the login restriction for files-only directories or adding an optional directory password to the CWD command.
tldr.outcome: The note presents alternatives for discussion and says anonymous users should not be allowed to use the password mechanism to change their access.

facts.label: Existing CWD command
facts.value: Changes working directory without granting owner access

today: The unit records RFC 697's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It is a proposal about FTP access to TENEX files-only directories.

sections.title: TENEX Files-Only Directories
sections.content:
TENEX distinguishes logging in to a directory from connecting to one. A login gives the directory owner access to a job and an address space; a connection gives an existing job access to the directory without creating an address space.

The TENEX FTP server does not allow an FTP login to a files-only directory. Its existing CWD command provides part of the connect function but does not give the user owner access, so the user cannot use the directory password to obtain owner rights through the current FTP commands.
sections.plainLanguage: TENEX can connect a job to a files-only directory, but its FTP login does not give the user owner access there. The current CWD command does not solve that problem.

sections.title: Two Proposed Changes
sections.content:
The first proposal removes the restriction that prevents FTP login to files-only directories. Under that approach, a network user who knows the directory password would count as its owner for FTP purposes.

The second proposal adds an optional password argument to CWD. If the password matches, the user receives owner rights to the directory. If it is absent or fails, CWD works as it does under the current protection mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: One option allows FTP login to a files-only directory with its password. The other keeps the existing login rule and lets CWD accept a directory password.

sections.title: Access-Control Trade-Off
sections.content:
The author frames the choice around how FTP should treat the relationship between a directory password and owner access. If knowing the password is enough to count as the owner in FTP, the login restriction can be removed; if FTP login should remain as restrictive as a user login, a separate connect-style command is needed.

The proposal explicitly says anonymous users should not be allowed to use the password mechanism to change their access to the file system.
sections.plainLanguage: The choice is whether a directory password grants owner access during FTP login or only through an added CWD option. The note excludes anonymous users from that access change.
